displayQuote: A little learning is a dangerous thing

meta.title: Who really said "A little learning is a dangerous thing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Alexander Pope wrote it in An Essay on Criticism (1711). The common "a little knowledge" version is a later misquote of his line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A little learning is a dangerous thing'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Alexander Pope, from An Essay on Criticism (1711). The popular "a little knowledge is a dangerous thing" is a misquote.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Pope wrote this line in An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II. His original spelling was “A little learning is a dang’rous thing” — the widely-seen “a little knowledge is a dangerous thing” is a later misquote.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
A little learning is a dang’rous thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring:
There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain,
And drinking largely sobers us again.
trail: The line opens the second part of Pope’s An Essay on Criticism, first published anonymously in 1711.
Wikipedia records the original as “A little learning is a dang’rous thing” and notes it is “frequently paraphrased as ‘A little knowledge is a dangerous thing’” (source).
Quote Investigator quotes Pope’s couplet verbatim while untangling a separate, later saying about “false knowledge.”
Word historians at Phrases.org.uk trace the “knowledge” swap to an 18th-century misquotation of Pope.
source.excerptNote: Pope’s point is that a smattering of study is more dangerous than none, because it breeds false confidence — the cure is to “drink deep” from the Pierian spring, the classical fountain of the Muses.

author.name: Alexander Pope
author.heading: About Alexander Pope
author.bio: Alexander Pope was the leading English poet of the early 18th century, celebrated for his polished heroic couplets and biting satire in works such as The Rape of the Lock and The Dunciad. His verse essays — including An Essay on Criticism (1711) and An Essay on Man — packed memorable maxims into rhyme, which is why so many everyday English phrases trace back to him. He is one of the most-quoted writers in the language.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Pope is correct — the trouble is the wording, which is very often altered or handed to the wrong person.

items.who: “A little knowledge is a dangerous thing”
items.why: Pope wrote “learning,” not “knowledge.” The “knowledge” version is a paraphrase that took hold through 18th-century misquotation and is now more common than the original (Phrases.org.uk).
Bacon expressed a kindred thought about shallow versus deep study in his essay Of Atheism (1601), and the idea is sometimes traced to him — but the memorable line itself is Pope’s (Phrases.org.uk).

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Pope, from An Essay on Criticism (1711) — but the original word is “learning,” and the spelling was “dang’rous.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Pope was barely 23 when An Essay on Criticism appeared, a verse manifesto on how to judge literature. The line sits at the head of its second part, warning would-be critics that a shallow acquaintance with learning is worse than none: it produces confident fools.

The poem is a quarry of familiar English phrases — “To err is human, to forgive divine” and “Fools rush in where angels fear to tread” also come from it — which is part of why this line has stayed in circulation for three centuries.
